design_detail: Naturalistic field study of two self-selected parallel groups, each tested twice, without any measurement before ketamine use: 20 people who said they had taken ketamine that evening, within 30 minutes before testing, and 19 people from the same private parties or nightclub who said they had not taken it that evening and had little or no ketamine history. Day 0: tested in a small quiet room at the party or club, the ketamine group while intoxicated; day 3: retested at home. The same 25–35-minute battery in the same order on both days (prose recall, letter and category fluency, speed of comprehension, serial sevens, word-stem completion, digit cancellation; self-rated dissociation, state schizotypy, mood, 14 drug-symptom ratings, HADS), with alternate versions balanced across groups. Participants were young people who use drugs recreationally, tested where they were using them; neither laboratory volunteers given a known dose nor patients. Repeated-measures ANOVA, group (between) by day (within). Classed as a short prospective cohort, as for the same laboratory's MDMA field study (sc_curran_1997); the day-3 contrast is in effect a cross-sectional comparison of people who use ketamine with polydrug-using peers who mostly do not.
can_establish: How 20 people tested within 30 minutes of self-reported ketamine use at a party or club differed from 19 polydrug-using peers in the same settings on memory, attention, self-rated dissociation, psychosis-like experiences, mood and bodily symptoms that night, and how the two groups compared when retested at home 3 days later.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused the differences still present on day 3 (there was no measurement before use, intake was self-reported and unverified, and the comparison group, with little or no ketamine history, differed in education, past antidepressant prescription and HADS depression covering the two days up to the drug night); whether any difference lasts beyond 3 days; how large the differences are against test norms; or what known amounts of pure ketamine do.

sample.recruitment: Community: volunteers approached at private parties or a nightclub and recruited by snowball sampling (p. 577); the city, number of venues and recruitment period are not reported. On day 0 people were tested in a small, quiet side room at the venue; on day 3 at home, in the quietest room available (p. 578).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All used several drugs, by the authors' description. People who reported having used drugs other than ketamine, cannabis or small amounts of alcohol or MDMA before the day-0 testing were not included. Ketamine group: had taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before taking part. Comparison group: had not taken ketamine that evening and had little or no previous use (p. 577). Data from two people who took drugs on the day of the second session were discarded (p. 578). No age, psychiatric or medical criteria are stated.
sample.demographics: 23 men and 16 women aged 18–29 (mean 22.7, SD 2.3); the sex split by group is not reported (p. 577). Mean age 23.2 (SD 2.5) in the ketamine group and 22.1 (SD 1.9) in the comparison group. University-level education (studying for or holding a degree): 15 of 20 against 18 of 19; of the rest, 3 in the ketamine group had A-levels and 2 GCSEs, and 1 control had GCSEs (p. 579). Four of the ketamine group and one control had been prescribed antidepressants in the past; none was taking prescribed medication (p. 581).
sample.attrition: Seven more people tested on day 0 were not available for retesting and data from two more were discarded because they took drugs on the day of the second session, so 39 of 48 tested on day 0 were analysed (81%, editors' arithmetic); the groups of the nine are not reported and completers are not compared with them (pp. 577–578). The HADS depression test has 32 error degrees of freedom, implying 34 participants, without explanation (p. 585).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected, mostly university-educated volunteers willing to be tested at a party or club, grouped by what they said they had taken that night. The ketamine group used ketamine from monthly to twice weekly, while only 4 of 19 controls had ever tried it (21%), so on day 3 the comparison is between people who use ketamine and polydrug-using peers who mostly do not, with whatever else distinguishes people who choose ketamine. University education (75% against 95%), past antidepressant prescription (4 against 1) and higher HADS depression already on day 0 point to differences that predate the test night.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only. Group membership rested on what people said on day 0; on day 3 everyone in the ketamine group again reported day-0 use, and a retrospective account of day-0 use and a general drug history were recorded (pp. 578–579). A hair sample was taken on day 3 and participants were told it could be analysed to confirm their drug use, but it was not analysed because the resources were not available (pp. 578, 588). No urine, blood or drug-sample testing; the authors take the close match between the acute effects they observed and laboratory findings as support that reported use was accurate (p. 588).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported by participants, not amounts given by the study: the amounts taken before the day-0 testing ranged from 0.0625 g to 0.5 g (mean 0.14 g, SD 0.16), of unknown content; route and number of separate doses were not recorded; testing began within 30 minutes of use; 36% of the ketamine group took more ketamine after the testing that night and none on days 1–3 (pp. 579–580). The authors equate the mean amount with about 2 mg/kg (p. 585). Usual frequency in the ketamine group: twice a week 12%, once a week 29%, once every 2 weeks 47%, once a month 12%; duration of use under 1 year 35%, 1–2 years 47%, over 2 years 18% (p. 580).
exposure.polysubstance: Day 0: cannabis smoked by all 20 in the ketamine group and 17 of 19 controls, with a similar number of joints (amount unknown); alcohol by 65% of the ketamine group (mean 1.1 units, range 0–6) and 72% of controls (mean 1.8, range 0–4), all more than 2 hours before testing; a quarter of an MDMA tablet more than 4 hours before testing in 2 of the ketamine group and 1 control (p. 580). Between sessions everyone reported alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1 and 2, at similar levels in both groups, and none on day 3 (p. 580). History: both groups were described as using cannabis and alcohol from twice a week to daily and MDMA and amphetamine from fortnightly to monthly; LSD and cocaine were used regularly by several participants; heroin, psilocybin, DMT, 2C-B and temazepam had been used by several, PCP tried by 2 and scopolamine by 1 (pp. 580–581). No group-wise figures or tests are given and nothing is adjusted.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Day 0 was measured during intoxication (ketamine within the previous 30 minutes, cannabis in 37 of 39, alcohol more than 2 hours earlier in most). Day 3: participants were asked to take no illicit substances for 3 days; by their own report the ketamine group took no ketamine on days 1–3 and nobody took alcohol or cannabis on day 3; nothing was verified (pp. 578, 580).

comparison.controls: 19 volunteers recruited in the same party and club settings who had not taken ketamine that evening and had little or no ketamine history (4 had tried it, none used it regularly) and who, by their own account, used a similar range of other drugs (pp. 577, 581). They were tested on the same schedule; on day 0 most had smoked cannabis (17 of 19) and drunk alcohol (72%).
comparison.matching: No formal matching or adjustment. Similar mean age (23.2 against 22.1). Education is described by the authors as similar and well matched, but university level was 15 of 20 against 18 of 19 (editors' Fisher exact test p = 0.18; a 20-point difference in a small sample). Sex by group not reported; other drug use described as similar without figures.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measurement before ketamine use, and no estimate of premorbid IQ or verbal ability. Psychiatric history only as past antidepressant prescription (4 against 1). The day-0 HADS, rated for the preceding two days, already showed higher depression in the ketamine group (4.45 against 1.89), for a period that ended with that night's drug use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: People who use several drugs: cannabis and alcohol on the test night in most of them, and regular cannabis, alcohol, MDMA and amphetamine use described as similar to the ketamine group's, without figures.

outcomes.instruments: Same order on both days; day 0 in the quiet room at the party or club, during the ketamine group's intoxication; day 3 at home. Cognitive tests (p. 578): Rivermead prose passage, recalled immediately and after a 15-minute filled delay (episodic memory; one point per idea, half points for partial recall; maximum 21); letter fluency (R or M) and category fluency (fruit, vegetables), 90 s each, correct words and errors (semantic memory, frontal function); speed of comprehension test (SComp: judging as many of 100 sentences as sensible or not as possible in 2 minutes; semantic memory); serial sevens for 90 s (working memory); word-stem completion of 32 stems about 3 minutes after rating 20 words (implicit memory, priming); digit cancellation, deleting 40 target digits among 400 (focused attention), time and errors. Self-ratings (p. 579): adapted CADSS, the 19 self-rated items of the Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale, each rated 1–5, with the 8 clinician-observed items dropped (depersonalization, derealization, amnesia); Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire, 30 items constructed for this study from the Schizotypal Personality Questionnaire and the Magical Ideation Scale and reworded from trait to state (true for you "at this moment"), each rated 1–5, with a total and perceptual distortion, magical ideation and thought disorder subscores (items in the Appendix, p. 590); Bond–Lader mood scale (16 visual analogue scales; alertness, contentedness, calmness); Subjective Effects Scale (14 visual analogue scales of symptoms induced by drugs like ketamine); Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale with the time frame changed from the last week to the last two days.
outcomes.validity_norms: No comparison with published norms for any test. The adapted CADSS and the state version of the schizotypy questionnaire are not validated; the authors call results on the questionnaire preliminary and say its items tap psychosis proneness rather than psychosis in a clinical sense (p. 587). Day 0–day 3 correlations in the comparison group were 0.93 for the dissociation scale and 0.94 for the schizotypy questionnaire (pp. 584–585), so both state scales behaved like stable traits in controls. The authors cite 8–11 as the clinically significant HADS range (p. 585), although the scale's time frame was altered.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impairment' means a lower score than the comparison group on the same day, and 'persisting' or 'residual' a group difference on day 3. To check whether a day-3 difference could be a missed practice benefit (people who remember little of the first session gain less from it), the ketamine group's day-3 scores were compared with the comparison group's day-0 scores (p. 579). Dissociation and psychosis-like experiences were self-rated only; the authors judged clinician-administered psychiatric ratings impracticable in this setting (p. 577).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. Editors' count: 14 cognitive scores (Table 1), 13 self-rating scores (Table 2) and 14 symptom ratings (Table 3), each tested for group, day and interaction. Significance was set at p<0.01 and post hoc t-tests were Bonferroni-corrected, the number of comparisons not stated (p. 579); correlations were computed without a stated number or correction. Effects at p between 0.01 and 0.05 are reported as trends and some are interpreted (letter fluency; self-rated memory on day 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Group was evident to the tester on day 0, since people were recruited according to whether they had just taken ketamine; prose recall scoring involves judgment (half points for incomplete recall or close synonyms), and who scored it, and whether blind, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: The paper gives F values (df 1,37) and p values, without effect sizes or confidence intervals. Editors' calculation from Tables 1 and 2 (independent t-tests with pooled SD, n 20 and 19; Hedges' g with approximate 95% CI; negative = ketamine group lower). Day 0, during intoxication: immediate prose recall g −1.97 (−2.74 to −1.21); delayed recall −1.68 (−2.42 to −0.95); speed of comprehension −1.86 (−2.61 to −1.11); serial sevens −1.53 (−2.25 to −0.82); category fluency −1.31 (−2.00 to −0.62); letter fluency −1.04 (−1.71 to −0.37); cancellation time +0.94 (0.28 to 1.61, slower); word-stem targets −0.29 (−0.92 to 0.34). Day 3: immediate recall −0.93 (−1.59 to −0.27); delayed recall −1.01 (−1.68 to −0.34); category fluency −1.22 (−1.90 to −0.53); speed of comprehension −0.86 (−1.51 to −0.20), t(37) = 2.74, p ≈ 0.0095; letter fluency −0.42 (−1.05 to 0.22); serial sevens −0.24 (−0.87 to 0.39); cancellation time +0.05 (−0.58 to 0.68). Self-ratings, day 0 then day 3: dissociation total 3.50 (2.50 to 4.50) and 0.90 (0.24 to 1.56); schizotypal total 2.77 (1.89 to 3.65) and 1.52 (0.81 to 2.24); magical ideation 2.21 and 1.44; HADS depression 1.43 (0.72 to 2.13) and 1.25 (0.56 to 1.93); HADS anxiety 0.19 and 0.16. The authors' practice check (ketamine group on day 3 against controls on day 0), recomputed the same way: speed of comprehension t(37) = 2.11, p ≈ 0.04 (printed p<0.009); category fluency t(37) = 2.07, p ≈ 0.046 (printed as not significant); immediate recall t(37) = 1.15, p ≈ 0.26.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted repeated-measures ANOVA with post hoc t-tests.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (submitted July 1999).
analysis.selective_reporting: Same-day post hoc tests on day 3 are reported for the dissociation and schizotypy scores but for none of the cognitive tests, so the day-3 group difference on each test is never tested directly in the paper (the practice check is reported instead). Correlations are reported only where significant, without the number computed, and the Results do not say clearly which participants entered the day-3 correlations. Several day-3 cells have SDs about as large as their means (dissociation 17.75, SD 17.41), but no distributions or individual data are shown.
analysis.power: Not reported. Editors' calculation: with 20 and 19 per group, a two-sided test has 80% power for a standardized difference of about 0.92 at alpha 0.05 and about 1.15 at the paper's alpha of 0.01, so day-3 differences of the size observed (about 0.9) were at the edge of detectability, and the null day-3 results (serial sevens, cancellation, letter fluency) do not show that the groups were alike.

interpretation_gap.results_show: On the night of use, people tested within 30 minutes of self-reported ketamine use performed far worse than polydrug-using peers on prose recall, both fluency tasks, speed of comprehension, serial sevens and cancellation (editors' standardized differences about 0.9 to 2.0), but not on word-stem priming, and rated much higher dissociation, psychosis-like experiences and bodily and perceptual symptoms. Three days later serial sevens and cancellation no longer differed; prose recall and category fluency were still lower, but the ketamine group's day-3 scores did not differ significantly from the controls' day-0 scores, which the authors read, for recall, as a missed practice benefit; speed of comprehension was still lower (editors' p ≈ 0.01). On day 3 the ketamine group still rated more dissociation (17.75 against 5.37) and schizotypal symptoms (62.35 against 26.42, largest on magical ideation), and its HADS depression was higher on both days (about 4.4 against 1.8), below the clinical range the authors cite.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that on semantic-memory tests the ketamine group showed persisting impairments, and concludes that "Ketamine appears to induce acute and severe impairments of working, episodic and semantic memory" (p. 575); it also says the day-3 differences could reflect chronic or residual effects or pre-existing differences. The Discussion calls the day-3 differences "an important and worrying finding" given close matching for polydrug use, age and education (p. 585), and argues that pre-existing differences are unlikely to be the only factor (p. 587). Gaps: (1) the persisting semantic-memory deficit rests on speed of comprehension, whose practice check is printed as p<0.009 but gives p ≈ 0.04 from Table 1, and on category fluency, whose practice check the Results report as not significant (p. 584) while the Discussion lists it as worse on both days (p. 586); (2) the groups were not closely matched: university education 75% against 95%, past antidepressants 4 against 1, HADS depression higher already for the two days up to the drug night, and similarity of drug use asserted without figures; (3) 'impairment' is relative to this comparison group only, without norms; (4) the day-3 dissociation and schizotypy differences come from self-rated scales, one unvalidated, that behaved as stable traits in controls (test–retest 0.93 and 0.94), and the magical-ideation items that carry much of the schizotypy difference are statements of belief (for example about telepathy, reincarnation and spirits, Appendix, p. 590), so a stable difference between people who choose ketamine and people who do not explains them as well as a residual drug effect; the authors concede that their data cannot tell these apart (p. 587); (5) the comparison of the self-reported amount (about 2 mg/kg) with the 0.1–1.0 mg/kg of laboratory studies (p. 585) does not allow for unknown purity and states the route of neither.

timeline.event: This study: the first report of cognitive and psychological measures in people who use ketamine, taken on a night of use and 3 days later, against polydrug-using peers from the same settings.

Curran and Monaghan, same laboratory and battery: 18 people who used ketamine more than twice a month against 19 who used it less, all tested on a night of use and 3 days later. The acute profile was reproduced in both groups, but neither group had raised dissociation or schizotypal scores on day 3 (both low); prose recall and category fluency were lower in the frequent group on day 3. That paper gives this study's ketamine group an average use of 3.1 times a month, a figure not printed here.

Three-year longitudinal follow-up by the same group of people who had substantially reduced their ketamine use (per its title; Morgan, Monaghan and Curran, 2004); results to be taken from its own card.
Comparison of frequent, infrequent and former ketamine use with polydrug-using and non-using controls (per its title; Morgan, Muetzelfeldt and Curran, 2009); results to be taken from its own card.

One-year longitudinal study of neurocognitive function and psychological wellbeing with chronic ketamine self-administration (per its title; Morgan, Muetzelfeldt and Curran, 2010), which has a published erratum; results to be taken from its own card.
Narrative review of ketamine use for the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs (Morgan and Curran, 2012); to be checked for how it summarizes this study.

replication.where_it_stands: The acute (day-0) profile was reproduced by the same laboratory's second field study (Curran and Monaghan, 2001) and, by the authors' account, agrees with laboratory studies of single doses in volunteers. The day-3 elevation of dissociation and schizotypal scores was not found in either group of the 2001 study, whose authors suggest a U-shaped relation with frequency of use or differences between the samples (here mainly nightclubs and 75% university-educated; there mainly squat parties). Whether people who use ketamine have poorer semantic memory some days after use, and why, is examined by the same group's later studies listed above, to be appraised on their own cards; this study alone cannot separate a drug effect from pre-existing differences.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no acknowledgements, funding statement or competing-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Psychopharmacology Research Unit, Department of Psychology, University College London (correspondence address, p. 575).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people from the same party and club scene, measured before they start using ketamine or after a verified ketamine-free period, then on a night of use and repeatedly over the following weeks, with use confirmed by hair or urine analysis, testers blind to group, validated state measures of dissociation and psychotic-like experiences, memory tests scored against norms, and a comparison group matched on education and psychiatric history that is retested on the same schedule.

domains.note: No measurement before use; groups formed by what people chose to take that night, against a comparison group with little or no ketamine history; differences in university education (75% against 95%), past antidepressant prescription (4 against 1) and HADS depression already on day 0; other drug use asserted to be similar without figures; sex by group unknown; nothing adjusted. Less of a concern for the day-0 (acute) contrast, since both groups came from the same settings and most had also used cannabis.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Self-report only; hair samples taken but not analysed; amounts of unknown content by an unrecorded route; further use after testing in 36% of the ketamine group; usual-use percentages that appear to rest on 17 of the 20.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Snowball recruitment at parties and a nightclub of volunteers willing to be tested while intoxicated, grouped by what they chose to take that night.
Between sessions, further ketamine after the day-0 testing in 36% of the ketamine group and alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1–2 in everyone; abstinence on day 3 self-reported and not verified.
39 of 48 tested on day 0 analysed (81%); the groups of those lost are not reported and completers are not compared with them; HADS depression analysed in 34.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Tester not blind (group evident on day 0); self-ratings completed during intoxication on day 0, one questionnaire built for this study and unvalidated, the CADSS used without its clinician-observed items, the HADS time frame changed, and reported means below the stated scale minima; setting changed with the day (party or club against home).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: 41 measures with three tests each; alpha set at 0.01 but trends interpreted; same-day day-3 tests reported only for the self-ratings; only significant correlations reported; the practice check behind the semantic-memory conclusion is printed as p<0.009 for speed of comprehension but gives p ≈ 0.04 from the printed means and SDs, while an equally strong check for category fluency is reported as not significant.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The study can be cited for the size and profile of acute cognitive, dissociative and bodily effects in people tested within 30 minutes of self-reported ketamine use at a party or club, compared with polydrug-using peers in the same setting; for that day-0 contrast the risk of bias is high rather than very high (self-reported, unverified exposure and an unblinded tester, but large effects that the companion study reproduced). It cannot be cited as showing that ketamine causes semantic-memory deficits, dissociation or schizotypal symptoms 3 days after use: there is no baseline, the comparison group differs in ketamine history, education and psychiatric indicators, the symptom scales are self-rated and partly unvalidated, and the practice check that underpins the semantic-memory conclusion does not reproduce from the paper's own table. Very high risk of bias for any causal reading of the day-3 differences.

key_findings.finding: Design and timing: 39 people were analysed, 20 who said they had taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before testing and 19 from the same settings who had not taken it that evening and had little or no ketamine history. Both groups were tested on the night of recruitment (day 0) in a quiet room at the party or club and again 3 days later (day 3) at home, with the same 25–35-minute battery in the same order. Seven more people tested on day 0 were not retested and data from two were discarded for drug use on the day of the second session.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Design and participants (p. 575); Methods › Participants and design, 1st paragraph (p. 577, continuing on p. 578); Procedure, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 578)

key_findings.finding: Ketamine use was established by self-report only: when asked again on day 3, everyone in the ketamine group reported day-0 use. Reported amounts taken before the day-0 testing ranged from 0.0625 g to 0.5 g (mean 0.14 g, SD 0.16), of unknown content and by an unrecorded route, and 36% of the ketamine group took more after the testing that night. Hair samples were collected on day 3 but never analysed.
key_findings.locator: Procedure, 3rd paragraph (p. 578); Results › Demographics and drug use › Reported drug use on day 0 (paragraph beginning on p. 579, continuing on p. 580); Discussion, limitations paragraph (p. 588)
key_findings.note: Self-reported amounts are study conditions, not doses given by the study. The authors equate the mean with about 2 mg/kg and compare it with 0.1–1.0 mg/kg in laboratory studies (p. 585), without allowing for purity or stating the route of either.

key_findings.finding: Other drugs on the test night: cannabis in all 20 of the ketamine group and 17 controls; alcohol in 65% of the ketamine group (mean 1.1 units, range 0–6) and 72% of controls (mean 1.8, range 0–4), all more than 2 hours before testing; a quarter of an MDMA tablet more than 4 hours before testing in 2 of the ketamine group and 1 control. Everyone reported alcohol and/or cannabis on days 1 and 2, at similar levels, and none on day 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics and drug use › Reported drug use on day 0 (paragraph beginning on p. 579; these figures on p. 580, left and right columns)

key_findings.finding: University-level education (studying for or holding a degree) in 15 of 20 in the ketamine group and 18 of 19 controls, which the authors call similar; past antidepressant prescription in 4 of the ketamine group and 1 control, none on current medication. Mean age 23.2 (SD 2.5) and 22.1 (SD 1.9); sex by group not reported.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics and drug use, 1st paragraph (p. 579); Reported general drug use, end of the paragraph (p. 581, right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' Fisher exact test for education: p = 0.18.

key_findings.finding: Usual ketamine use in the ketamine group: twice a week 12%, once a week 29%, once every 2 weeks 47%, once a month 12%; for under 1 year 35%, 1–2 years 47%, over 2 years 18%. In the comparison group 21% had tried ketamine and none used it regularly. Both groups were described as using cannabis and alcohol from twice a week to daily and MDMA and amphetamine from fortnightly to monthly, without group-wise figures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics and drug use › Reported general drug use (p. 580, right column, continuing on p. 581)
key_findings.note: The ketamine-group percentages are whole-number shares of 17 people (2, 5, 8, 2 and 6, 8, 3), not of 20 (editors' arithmetic), so drug-history data appear to be missing for 3 people without comment.

key_findings.finding: Acute effects (day 0, within 30 minutes of reported use), ketamine group against controls, means (SD): immediate prose recall 3.83 (2.17) against 8.61 (2.57); delayed recall 2.48 (1.50) against 6.87 (3.32); category fluency 11.20 (4.38) against 17.74 (5.39); letter fluency 16.00 (4.59) against 21.32 (5.42); speed of comprehension 42.35 (13.33) against 76.05 (21.45) sentences; serial sevens 10.8 (6.56) against 22.37 (8.19) correct; cancellation time 69.90 (18.46) against 54.92 (11.66) s; word-stem completion targets 3.00 (1.95) against 3.58 (2.01), with no group difference on that task.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, day 0 columns (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks › Word-stem completion (p. 584)
key_findings.note: Letter fluency: the paper's own tests for this task were trends at its p<0.01, and no day-0 post hoc test is reported (reporting issue 9).

key_findings.finding: Three days later (day 3), means (SD): serial sevens 21.30 (8.31) against 23.37 (8.37) and cancellation time 58.45 (9.51) against 57.96 (9.44), no longer different (group × day interactions F(1,37) = 13.6 and 15.0, both p<0.001); immediate prose recall 7.75 (2.08) against 10.18 (2.99) and delayed recall 6.73 (2.55) against 9.76 (3.30), still lower; letter fluency 18.90 (6.09) against 21.32 (5.28).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, day 3 columns (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks › Serial sevens and Digit cancellation task (p. 584)

key_findings.finding: Prose recall over days: immediate recall showed a group × day interaction (F(1,37) = 7.55, p<0.009) and main effects of day (F = 41.6) and group (F = 29.2); delayed recall showed group (F = 23.7) and day (F = 64.9) effects without an interaction. The ketamine group's day-3 immediate recall did not differ significantly from the controls' day-0 score, and the authors conclude that the day-3 recall differences most likely reflect a missed practice benefit caused by the drug's amnestic effect on day 0.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks (Table 1) › Prose recall (p. 581, right column, continuing on p. 583); Discussion › Cognitive effects, paragraph on group differences in prose recall (p. 586, right column)

key_findings.finding: Semantic-memory tests: category fluency was lower in the ketamine group on both days (group F(1,37) = 21.1, p<0.001; day-3 means 14.85 (3.08) against 19.68 (4.58)), with no interaction, and the ketamine group's day-3 score did not differ significantly from the controls' day-0 score. Speed of comprehension showed a group × day interaction (F = 28.9, p<0.001); the ketamine group judged fewer sentences on both days (day 3: 63.30 (16.04) against 79.11 (19.94)), and its day-3 score was reported as significantly below the controls' day-0 score (p<0.009).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 580); Results › Cognitive tasks › Category generation (p. 583, right column, continuing on p. 584) and Speed of comprehension test (p. 584, left column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1 (independent t-test, pooled SD, n 20 and 19): the speed-of-comprehension practice check gives t(37) = 2.11, p ≈ 0.04, and the category-fluency check t(37) = 2.07, p ≈ 0.046; the two are nearly identical, yet one is printed as p<0.009 and the other as not significant. The same-day day-3 speed-of-comprehension difference gives t(37) = 2.74, p ≈ 0.0095, g = −0.86 (−1.51 to −0.20).

key_findings.finding: Dissociation (adapted CADSS, self-rated): ketamine group 44.00 (13.98) against controls 5.47 (5.71) on day 0, and 17.75 (17.41) against 5.37 (7.21) on day 3; group × day interaction F(1,37) = 51.3, group F = 54.4, day F = 52.1 (all p<0.001); the day-3 difference was significant on post hoc test (p<0.008), with the same pattern for the depersonalization, derealization and amnesia factors. The controls' day 0–day 3 correlation was 0.93.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 581); Results › Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology (Table 2) › Dissociative States Scale (p. 584, right column)
key_findings.note: The ketamine group's day-3 SD (17.41) is about as large as its mean (17.75) on a total that cannot fall below zero, so the day-3 scores are skewed and a few people may carry the group difference; read the parametric post hoc test (p<0.008) with that in mind (editors' t-test on the day-3 cells p ≈ 0.007).

key_findings.finding: State schizotypal symptoms (questionnaire built for this study): 87.40 (16.21) against 33.37 (21.71) on day 0 and 62.35 (25.35) against 26.42 (20.45) on day 3; group × day interaction F(1,37) = 14.0, p = 0.001; day-3 difference p<0.001. Day-3 subscores: magical ideation 28.25 (12.75) against 11.00 (10.48) (day-3 difference p<0.001), perceptual distortion 10.40 (5.63) against 3.95 (4.54), thought disorder 14.80 (6.11) against 6.11 (4.98). The controls' day 0–day 3 correlation was 0.94.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 581); Results › Dissociation and schizotypal symptomatology › Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire (p. 584, right column, continuing on p. 585)

key_findings.finding: Drug-symptom ratings (14 visual analogue scales): on day 0 the ketamine group rated, for example, impaired memory 72.40 (19.58) against 16.63 (21.38), bodily numbness 60.30 (25.10) against 6.16 (9.63) and altered time perception 59.60 (28.37) against 9.79 (15.01); 11 of the 14 ratings showed group × day interactions; on day 3 the groups were similar except for a trend towards more self-rated impaired memory in the ketamine group (26.45 (25.13) against 11.95 (16.83), p<0.04).
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 582, printed sideways); Results › Mood and somatic measures › Subjective Effects Scale (p. 585, left column)

key_findings.finding: HADS depression (rated for the last two days) was higher in the ketamine group on both days: 4.45 (2.11) against 1.89 (1.29) on day 0 and 4.30 (2.58) against 1.68 (1.29) on day 3 (group F(1,32) = 19.4, p<0.001), below the clinically significant range of 8–11 the authors cite; anxiety did not differ (7.05 to 7.85 in all four cells). The mood scale showed only a trend for a day effect on contentedness (p<0.03).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 581); Results › Mood and somatic measures › Mood Rating Scale and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (p. 585, left column)

key_findings.finding: Within the ketamine group, the self-reported amount taken on day 0 did not correlate significantly with any cognitive score or with total schizotypy or dissociation. Day-3 dissociation correlated with day-3 errors on speed of comprehension (r = 0.67, p<0.001) and on category fluency (r = 0.58, p<0.01); schizotypy and dissociation correlated on day 3 (r = 0.59, p<0.01) but not on day 0.
key_findings.locator: Results › Correlations (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: With n = 20, r = 0.67 gives p ≈ 0.0012 and a 95% interval of 0.32 to 0.86 (editors' calculation, Fisher z); see reporting issues on which participants entered these correlations.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that their data cannot distinguish a cumulative or residual drug effect from pre-existing differences in dissociation and schizotypy, but argue that pre-existing differences are unlikely to be the only factor because the groups were matched for use of other drugs, education and day-3 attention; they also note that drugs and doses could not be confirmed objectively.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Dissociative, psychotogenic and subjective effects, 2nd paragraph (p. 587, left column, continuing in the right column); Discussion, limitations paragraph (p. 588)

reporting_issues.issue: The practice check for speed of comprehension (ketamine group on day 3 against controls on day 0) is reported as significant at p<0.009 (p. 584), while the same check for category fluency is reported as not significant (p. 584). By the editors' calculation (independent t-test with pooled SD) from the means and SDs in Table 1, the first gives t(37) = 2.11, p ≈ 0.04 (63.30, SD 16.04, n 20, against 76.05, SD 21.45, n 19) and the second almost the same, t(37) = 2.07, p ≈ 0.046.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's argument that a missed practice benefit cannot explain the day-3 speed-of-comprehension deficit, which the abstract's persisting semantic-memory impairment rests on, does not reproduce from its own table; under the paper's alpha of 0.01 or a Bonferroni correction neither check is significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Several printed p values do not match their F statistics with df (1,37): serial sevens group F = 7.2 is printed with p = 0.002 (editors' p ≈ 0.011) and day F = 11.3 with p = 0.01 (p ≈ 0.002), as if transposed; speed-of-comprehension errors group F = 12.1 with p = 0.01 (p ≈ 0.001) and day F = 6.1 with p = 0.01 (p ≈ 0.018); magical ideation interaction F = 10.0 with p = 0.005 (p ≈ 0.003).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but whether the serial-sevens group effect and the comprehension-error day effect meet the paper's own p<0.01 depends on which number is right; the F values, not the p values, should be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The adapted CADSS (19 items) and the schizotypy questionnaire (30 items) are described as rated from 1 to 5 and summed (p. 579), which gives minimum totals of 19 and 30, but the controls' dissociation means are 5.47 and 5.37 and their day-3 schizotypy total is 26.42; the magical-ideation subscore (13 items in the Appendix) has control means of 12.74 and 11.00, also below its minimum of 13.
reporting_issues.consequence: The items must have been scored from 0, or the scoring is misdescribed; absolute scale values cannot be interpreted or compared with other studies until this is resolved, though group differences are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Several percentages cannot be whole-number shares of the stated groups: the ketamine group's usual-frequency (12%, 29%, 47%, 12%) and duration (35%, 47%, 18%) figures fit 17 people, not 20; alcohol on day 0 in 72% of controls fits 18 people, not 19; and 36% of the ketamine group taking more ketamine after testing fits no group size from 17 to 20 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-use data appear to be missing for some participants without comment, so the exposure description of the ketamine group rests on fewer people than stated.

reporting_issues.issue: HADS depression is tested with F(1,32) (p. 585), while the other analyses have df (1,37); by the editors' arithmetic this implies 34 participants instead of 39.
reporting_issues.consequence: Five participants' HADS data are missing without explanation, and the group of the missing five is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports only a trend for a day effect on contentedness (p<0.03) for the mood scale (p. 585), but in Table 2 the alertness factor falls from 59.37 to 37.59 in the ketamine group and from 47.27 to 38.89 in controls, while contentedness changes less (24.25 to 29.98 and 31.80 to 34.56), and the day-0 alertness difference between groups is not mentioned. The direction of scoring of the factors is not stated; the companion study reads higher alertness-factor scores as more sedation (Curran and Monaghan, 2001, p. 755). Editors' calculation: pooled alertness falls from about 53.5 to 38.2 and pooled contentedness rises from about 27.9 to 32.2; the day-0 alertness difference gives t(37) = 2.93, p ≈ 0.006.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mood results in the text and in Table 2 cannot both be right as printed; claims about mood after ketamine should not rest on this paper's mood-scale text.

reporting_issues.issue: The day-3 correlations of dissociation with error scores (r = 0.67, p<0.001; r = 0.58, p<0.01) are not assigned to a sample in the Results (p. 585); the Discussion assigns them to the ketamine group (p. 586). By the editors' calculation, with n = 20 r = 0.67 gives p ≈ 0.0012, while the printed p<0.001 would fit all 39 participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: If the correlations pooled both groups, they partly restate the group difference rather than a within-group relation; the paper's support for linking residual semantic errors to dissociation is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The Appendix labels items 23 and 24 'H' and item 25 'P', codes not defined in its key, and marks item 18 with an asterisk that is not explained (presumably reverse-scored); the Methods say that just two items loaded on ideas of reference or paranoid ideation, while the Appendix codes two items IR and two Par or P.
reporting_issues.consequence: The composition and scoring of the subscores cannot be reproduced exactly from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Several text citations do not match the reference list: Lahti et al. 1993 (p. 576) against 1995 in the list; Bond and Lader 1984 (p. 579) against 1974; Ashton and Young 1998 (p. 577) against 1999; Javitt and Dukin (p. 577) against Javitt and Zukin; McKenna, Montimer and Hodges 1994 (p. 586) against McKenna, Mortimer and Hodges 1992; the Rivermead test's authors are misspelt (p. 578).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the data; sources should be traced through the reference list.

reporting_issues.issue: Letter fluency: the paper's own analysis of this task reached only trend level at its significance level of p<0.01 (group F(1,37) = 6.0, p = 0.019; group × day F(1,37) = 4.4, p = 0.04; p. 583), and no day-0 post hoc test is reported for it, yet the Discussion lists letter fluency among the tasks on which the ketamine group was very markedly impaired on the night (p. 585).
reporting_issues.consequence: The night-of-use letter-fluency deficit rests on the Table 1 means (editors' t-test on the day-0 cells, t(37) = 3.31, p ≈ 0.002, g −1.04; analysis field), not on a test the paper reports as significant; cite it with that caveat.
